milestones.claim: Atom Computing announced a 1,225-site atomic array populated with 1,180 qubits; the peer-reviewed paper describing the assembly method reports near-deterministic filling (99% per-site occupancy) of 1225-site arrays.

evidence.quote: Atom Computing announced it has created a 1,225-site atomic array, currently populated with 1,180 qubits, in its next-generation quantum computing platform.
We apply this protocol to demonstrate near-deterministic filling (99% per-site occupancy) of 1225-site arrays of optical traps.
evidence.locator: Crossref metadata record (api.crossref.org/works/<doi>), abstract; publisher page refused automated access (HTTP 403)

evidence.quote: We apply this protocol to demonstrate near-deterministic filling (99% per-site occupancy) of 1225-site arrays of optical traps.

milestones.claim: Atom Computing researchers report nuclear-spin qubits in 87Sr atoms with an echo coherence time of (40 ± 7) seconds while driving multiple qubits in parallel.

evidence.quote: Here we introduce a qubit encoded in two nuclear spin states of a single 87 Sr atom and demonstrate coherence approaching the minute-scale within an assembled register of individually-controlled qubits.
we observe coherence in excess of 10 5 times the current length of the operations, with \({T}_{2}^{{{{{\mathrm{echo}}}}}}=\left(40\pm 7\right)\) seconds
evidence.locator: Abstract (LaTeX as rendered on the page)

evidence.quote: The company has achieved record coherence times by demonstrating its qubits can store quantum information for 40 seconds.

milestones.claim: Atom Computing reports mid-circuit, site-selective measurement in a 171Yb tweezer array with conditional refilling of ancilla sites to correct for atom loss while maintaining data-qubit coherence.

evidence.quote: Midcircuit Qubit Measurement and Rearrangement in a Yb 171 Atomic Array
evidence.locator: Crossref metadata record, title (no abstract deposited); publisher page refused automated access (HTTP 403)

evidence.quote: we perform conditional refilling of ancilla sites to correct for occasional atom loss, while maintaining the coherence of data qubits
https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevX.13.041034

milestones.claim: Microsoft and Atom Computing report entangling 24 encoded qubits ([[4,2,2]] code, 48 atoms) in a cat state and running the Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm on up to 28 encoded qubits in 112 atoms, on a 256-qubit Ytterbium-atom processor; the preprint describes these as “logical qubits”.

evidence.quote: We demonstrate fault-tolerant quantum computation on a quantum processor with 256 qubits, each an individual neutral Ytterbium atom.
We demonstrate the entanglement of 24 logical qubits encoded into 48 atoms
We also implement the Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm with up to 28 logical qubits encoded into 112 atoms, showing better-than-physical error rates.
The logical qubits are encoded with the J4, 2, 2K code into 48 physical qubits.
evidence.locator: Section on cat state (Fig. 5); "J4, 2, 2K" is how pdftotext renders the double-bracket notation [[4, 2, 2]]

evidence.quote: Twenty-eight logical qubits, created from 112 physical qubits, were used to perform successful computations based on the Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm.

milestones.claim: Atom Computing reports a two-qubit entangling gate fidelity of 99.72(3)% with postselection and 99.40(3)% without, on the ground-state nuclear-spin qubit of tweezer-trapped 171Yb atoms.

evidence.quote: We measure our two-qubit entangling gate fidelity to be 99.72(3)% (99.40(3)%) with (without) postselection.
evidence.locator: Crossref metadata record (api.crossref.org/works/<doi>), abstract; publisher page refused automated access (HTTP 403)

evidence.quote: operating on the ground-state nuclear-spin qubit in arrays of tweezer-trapped 171 Yb atoms

evidence.quote: with a 99.963(2)% single-qubit gate fidelity, and a 99.56(5)% two-qubit gate fidelity

milestones.claim: Atom Computing reports measuring, re-initializing and replacing a subset of atoms mid-computation while maintaining coherence in others, performing up to 41 rounds of syndrome extraction in a repetition code.

evidence.quote: We highlight this capability by performing up to 41 rounds of syndrome extraction in a repetition code
evidence.locator: Crossref metadata record (api.crossref.org/works/<doi>), abstract; publisher page refused automated access (HTTP 403)

evidence.quote: we demonstrate the ability to measure and reinitialize, and if necessary replace, a subset of atoms while maintaining coherence in other atoms

milestones.claim: Atom Computing reports many cycles of syndrome extraction in a toric code with replacement of lost qubits, characterising the logical error rate after up to 90 cycles and a lower absolute logical error rate for the larger of two code distances up to 8 rounds; the company calls it a “full demonstration of quantum error correction”.

evidence.quote: We characterize the logical error rate after up to 90 cycles, showing that logical information can be preserved through multiple rounds of qubit reloading.
Comparing two distances of the code up to 8 rounds of syndrome extraction shows a lower absolute logical error rate for the larger distance code.
Atom Computing today announced the industry’s first full demonstration of quantum error correction using a toric code.

milestones.claim: QuEra made Aquila, an analog neutral-atom processor offering up to 256 qubits, available on Amazon Braket.

evidence.quote: QuEra Computing today announced that Aquila, its neutral atom quantum computer, is now available via Amazon Braket
Today, Aquila offers users up to 256 qubits, with plans to scale to much higher numbers.

milestones.claim: Harvard, MIT and QuEra researchers report two-qubit entangling gates with 99.5% fidelity on up to 60 atoms in parallel.

evidence.quote: Here we report the realization of two-qubit entangling gates with 99.5% fidelity on up to 60 atoms in parallel, surpassing the surface-code threshold for error correction
QuEra Computing Inc., Boston, MA, USA

milestones.claim: A Harvard-led team with QuEra reports a programmable processor operating with up to 280 physical qubits, improvement of a two-qubit logic gate as surface-code distance increased from 3 to 7, and sampling circuits with up to 48 encoded qubits in [[8,3,2]] code blocks, which the paper calls “logical qubits”.

evidence.quote: Here we report the realization of a programmable quantum processor based on encoded logical qubits operating with up to 280 physical qubits.
we demonstrate improvement of a two-qubit logic gate by scaling surface-code 6 distance from d = 3 to d = 7
using 3D [[8,3,2]] code blocks 16 , 17 , we realize computationally complex sampling circuits 18 with up to 48 logical qubits entangled with hypercube connectivity
QuEra Computing Inc., Boston, MA, USA

milestones.claim: QuEra, Harvard and MIT researchers report distillation of magic states encoded in d = 3 and d = 5 colour codes on a neutral-atom computer, with output logical magic-state fidelity improved over the inputs; QuEra states the work ran on its Gemini computer.

evidence.quote: We demonstrate the distillation of magic states encoded in d = 3 and d = 5 colour codes, observing improvements in the logical fidelity of the output magic states compared with the input logical magic states.
This work, including the design, assembly and operation of the Gemini-class neutral-atom quantum computer, was supported by QuEra Computing.
Using QuEra’s Gemini neutral-atom computer, the team first grouped individual atoms into error-protected logical qubits.

milestones.claim: Harvard and MIT researchers report assembling and maintaining an array of over 3,000 atoms for more than 2 hours using continuous reloading at 300,000 atoms per second, while preserving stored qubit states.

evidence.quote: Using a reloading rate of 300,000 atoms in tweezers per second, we create over 30,000 initialized qubits per second, which we leverage to assemble and maintain an array of over 3,000 atoms for more than 2 hours.
we demonstrate persistent refilling of the array with atomic qubits in either a spin-polarized or a coherent superposition state while preserving the quantum state of stored qubits
In a breakthrough led by Harvard and MIT, researchers demonstrated a 3,000-qubit array operating continuously for over two hours

milestones.claim: A Harvard-led team with MIT and QuEra reports using reconfigurable arrays of up to 448 neutral atoms to study repeated error correction, reporting 2.14(13)x below-threshold performance with surface codes in a four-round characterization circuit; the paper is titled “A fault-tolerant neutral-atom architecture for universal quantum computation”.

evidence.quote: A fault-tolerant neutral-atom architecture for universal quantum computation
Here we use reconfigurable arrays of up to 448 neutral atoms to implement the key elements of a universal, fault-tolerant quantum processing architecture
demonstrating 2.14(13)x below-threshold performance in a four-round characterization circuit by leveraging atom loss detection and machine learning decoding
QuEra Computing, Boston, MA, USA

milestones.claim: QuEra states it completed its first on-premises installation, a Gemini-class system at AIST in Japan operating alongside the ABCI-Q supercomputer.

gaps.topic: Atom Computing: whether 2024 system-availability target was met
gaps.why: No primary document found stating the date the AC1000 / second-generation system became available to external users; target left "open".
gaps.would_need: Atom Computing or customer release stating first external availability / delivery date.

gaps.why: The 2026 preview states Atom is "designing Atom’s third-generation systems with 10,000 physical qubits" but gives no date, so no target was recorded.

gaps.topic: Atom Computing: physical location of AC1000 / second-generation systems
gaps.why: Documents place the 100-qubit prototype Phoenix in Berkeley (2022) and say the Boulder facility "will house future generations", but no document found explicitly placing the AC1000 systems used for the Microsoft or toric-code results at a site; system drawn at HQ.
gaps.would_need: Document naming the facility of the second-generation systems.

gaps.topic: Atom Computing / Microsoft logical-qubit paper peer review
gaps.why: arXiv:2411.11822 (v3, June 2025) shows no journal reference; no journal version found.

gaps.topic: QuEra 2024 and 2025 roadmap targets (10 and 30 encoded-qubit systems): met or missed
gaps.why: No QuEra document found that states whether the 2024 ten-logical-qubit product or the 2025 30-logical-qubit model was launched; the Dec 2025 review re-dates the third generation to 2026-2027. Targets left "open".
gaps.would_need: QuEra statement on launch of these products, or archived roadmap page versions (Wayback) showing the revision.

gaps.why: QuEra expected the NQCC testbed to be operational in early 2025; no fetched document confirms it is operating.
gaps.would_need: NQCC or QuEra release confirming installation/operation.
